items.answer: Yes. The Whisper model recognises many languages including Chinese and English, and handles mixed-language audio.

items.question: Why is the first run slower?
items.answer: The first transcription downloads the Whisper model in your browser; it is then cached and reused, so later runs are much faster.

items.question: Does image OCR upload my picture?
items.answer: No. Text recognition runs locally in your browser, so screenshots and photos are never uploaded to a server.

items.question: Does it recognise Chinese text?
items.answer: Yes. It reads languages such as Chinese and English, making it useful for text in screenshots, scans and photos.

items.question: What affects recognition accuracy?
items.answer: Sharp, high-contrast, well-aligned images work best; blurry or handwritten content lowers accuracy.

items.question: Does encrypting a PDF upload my file?
items.answer: No. Both encryption and decryption run locally in your browser, so contracts and IDs are never uploaded.

items.question: Can it remove an existing open password?
items.answer: Yes, but you must enter the correct original password first; only after it is verified can a password-free PDF be produced.

items.question: What permission restrictions are supported?
items.answer: Besides an open password, you can restrict actions like printing and copying to control how the document is used.

items.question: Does adding a watermark upload my PDF?
items.answer: No. The watermark is drawn and written into the PDF locally in your browser, with no upload to any server.

items.question: What watermark styles are available?
items.answer: You can position with a 3x3 grid, tile or diagonally tile the mark, and adjust text, opacity, rotation and spacing.

items.question: Is the watermark applied to every page?
items.answer: Yes. The text watermark is added to every page, ideal for stamping a whole document with copyright or a “confidential” mark.

items.question: Does PDF-to-image upload my file?
items.answer: No. Each page is rendered to an image locally in your browser, so the PDF is never uploaded.

items.question: Can I export both PNG and JPG?
items.answer: Yes. You can export each page as high-resolution PNG or JPG; PNG keeps transparency while JPG is smaller.

items.question: Does it export every page?
items.answer: Yes. By default every page of the PDF is exported as its own image, so you can save or re-edit them one by one.

items.question: Does the regex tester upload my text?
items.answer: No. Matching runs locally in your browser, so your test text is never uploaded.

items.question: Which flags and groups are supported?
items.answer: It supports common flags like g, i, m and s plus named capture groups, and highlights every match in your text.

items.question: Are there ready-made regex templates?
items.answer: Yes. Built-in templates for email, URL, phone numbers and more can be applied in one click and then tweaked.

items.question: Does it support seconds and milliseconds?
items.answer: Yes. It handles Unix timestamps at second, millisecond and microsecond precision and converts to and from dates.

items.question: Can I convert across time zones?
items.answer: Yes. Multiple time zones are supported, so the same timestamp can be shown in your local time or a chosen zone.

items.question: Can I convert timestamps in bulk?
items.answer: Yes. Paste multiple lines of timestamps to convert them all to dates at once, which is handy for log data.

items.question: Which UUID versions are supported?
items.answer: It generates UUID v1, v4 and v7 as well as NanoID, so you can pick time-ordered or fully random identifiers.

items.question: Can I generate many at once?
items.answer: Yes. Bulk generation is supported, with options for case and hyphen removal, ready to use as database keys.

items.question: Are the generated UUIDs uploaded?
items.answer: No. Every UUID is generated randomly in your browser and is never sent to a server or logged.

items.question: Which color formats can it convert between?
items.answer: It converts between HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV and CMYK; enter any one and the others update instantly.

items.question: Can I preview the color live?
items.answer: Yes. A swatch preview updates as you convert so you can confirm the final color at a glance.

items.question: Is the CMYK conversion accurate?
items.answer: CMYK uses a common approximate formula that is fine for previews; for exact print values rely on professional color management.

items.question: Does decoding a JWT upload my token?
items.answer: No. The header and payload are decoded locally in your browser, so the token is never uploaded and your credentials stay private.

items.question: Can it verify the JWT signature?
items.answer: Yes. You can supply a secret to verify an HS256 signature locally and confirm the token has not been tampered with.

items.question: Can I see the token's expiry?
items.answer: Yes. After decoding you can read standard claims like exp and iat in the payload to tell whether the token has expired.

items.question: Does Font Subset upload my font file?
items.answer: No. TTF and WOFF fonts are read, subset, and regenerated locally in your browser, so files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Why can the generated font still include extra glyphs?
items.answer: The font library keeps required base glyphs, composite glyph dependencies, and font tables so the subset font can load and render correctly.

items.question: Can I export TTF and WOFF at the same time?
items.answer: The tool currently generates one target format at a time. Switch the output format and generate again to get the matching TTF or WOFF file.

items.question: Does QR generation upload my text?
items.answer: No. QR codes are generated locally in your browser, so text is not sent to a server.

items.question: What content can I encode as a QR code?
items.answer: You can encode URLs, plain text, contact data, Wi-Fi configuration text, or any string that fits in a QR code. Longer text creates denser QR codes.

items.question: Does Info Encoder / Decoder upload my content to a server?
items.answer: No. Encoding, decoding, hashing, and parsing all run locally in your browser, so your input is not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Which formats does Info Encoder / Decoder support?
items.answer: It supports common text workflows such as Unicode, URL, UTF16, Base64, MD5, SHA1, hex, HTML entities, JWT, cookies, Gzip, URL parameters, and string escaping.

items.question: Does JWT decode also verify signatures?
items.answer: By default it only decodes the JWT header and payload so you can inspect the contents quickly. Signature verification is handled in the dedicated JWT tool.

items.question: Which Gzip inputs are supported?
items.answer: The tool accepts gzip data in Base64 or hex form and shows the decompressed result directly on the page for easy copying or follow-up processing.

items.question: What format does Word Merge export?
items.answer: It exports DOCX. The browser-based merge currently supports DOCX only, so legacy DOC files should be converted to DOCX first.

items.question: Does Word Merge upload my files?
items.answer: No. DOCX documents are unpacked, merged, and repacked locally in your browser.

items.question: What format does PPT Merge export?
items.answer: It exports PPTX. The browser-based merge currently supports PPTX only, so legacy PPT files should be converted to PPTX first.

items.question: Does PPT Merge preserve slide order?
items.answer: Yes. The output file appends slides from each PPTX in the order shown in the upload list.

items.question: How does TXT Merge separate file contents?
items.answer: The output TXT joins files in order and adds the source filename before each section.

items.question: Does Markdown Merge preserve Markdown syntax?
items.answer: Yes. It appends the original Markdown content in order and adds a second-level heading for each source file.

items.question: How does CSV Merge handle different headers?
items.answer: It keeps every column that appears across the source files and adds a source_file column.

items.question: Does RTF Merge preserve all rich text styling?
items.answer: The output is still an RTF file. The browser-based merge keeps readable text content and separates sections by source filename.

items.question: Which Excel merge modes are supported?
items.answer: You can combine all table data into one Sheet, or keep each source Sheet and export them in one workbook.

items.question: Does Excel Merge support CSV?
items.answer: Yes. CSV files are read as tables and can be merged together with Excel files.

items.question: Which output formats does Image Merge support?
items.answer: You can export one PDF or stitch multiple images vertically into a long PNG.

items.question: Does Image Merge compress the original images?
items.answer: Long images are rendered through the browser Canvas as PNG, and PDF output embeds images into pages without uploading them to a server.

items.question: Does QR decoding upload my image?
items.answer: No. Uploaded images and camera frames are read and decoded locally in your browser and are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Which image formats can be decoded?
items.answer: PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF, and BMP files are supported when your browser can read them. Clear, upright, high-contrast QR codes decode best.

items.question: What permission does live camera scanning need?
items.answer: After you click Start camera, the browser asks for camera permission. Once allowed, the page scans the video locally and updates the result automatically when a QR code is found.

items.question: Does Image Compressor upload my files?
items.answer: No. Compression runs locally in your browser, using Worker and OffscreenCanvas when available. Images are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: How does it choose the compression level automatically?
items.answer: For each image, the tool tries conservative quality levels for the selected output mode and compares pixel samples with the source. PNG files use color quantization by default; WebP is used only when the WebP option is enabled.

items.question: Why are some images marked as already near optimal?
items.answer: If the browser encoder cannot produce a smaller visually safe result, the original file is kept to avoid increasing file size or creating obvious quality loss.

items.question: Can I download compressed images in bulk?
items.answer: Yes. After multiple images finish compressing, you can download files individually or export all results as one ZIP archive.

items.question: Does Image Upscale upload files?
items.answer: No. Images are decoded, upscaled, and exported locally in your browser, so files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: What is pixel-perfect upscaling best for?
items.answer: It is best for icons, QR codes, screenshots, pixel art, and hard-edged graphics. It disables interpolation and enlarges pixels directly.

items.question: Which mode should I use for photos?
items.answer: Photos, gradients, and natural images usually work better with Smooth HD or Sharp enhance. Sharp enhance adds light sharpening so edges look clearer.

items.question: Does Sharp enhance generate new AI detail?
items.answer: No. Sharp enhance uses high-quality resampling and light sharpening to make existing edges and textures clearer, but it does not invent details that were not in the source image.

items.question: Why does the file get larger after upscaling?
items.answer: Upscaling increases the pixel count, and lossless formats such as PNG can become much larger. You can compress the result with Image Compressor afterward.

items.question: Does background removal upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are processed locally in your browser and are not uploaded to a server. The browser may download open-source model assets the first time you use it.

items.question: What format is the result?
items.answer: The output is a PNG file with an alpha channel, useful for further editing, design work, or conversion to formats such as WebP.

items.question: Why is the first run slower?
items.answer: The first run needs to load WASM and ONNX model assets. They are usually cached by the browser, so later runs in the same browser are faster.

items.question: Can it remove every complex background perfectly?
items.answer: The tool automatically detects the foreground and creates a transparent background, but hair, translucent materials, low-contrast edges, or similar foreground and background colors may still need manual retouching.

items.question: Does ID photo generation upload my photo?
items.answer: No. Image decoding, AI background removal, framing, and export all run locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server. The browser may download open-source model assets on first use.

items.question: Which ID photo sizes are supported?
items.answer: Built-in presets include China 1 inch, China 2 inch, China visa, 2 x 2 inch, EU / Schengen, Japan passport, and a custom millimeter-based canvas size.

items.question: What if the automatic face framing is not exact?
items.answer: The tool tries to detect the face and place the head near the 50% to 70% reference range. If face detection is unavailable, it falls back to the foreground subject bounds, and you can still drag and zoom manually.

items.question: Does watermark removal upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are decoded, inpainted with AI or repaired quickly, and exported locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server. The default high-quality AI downloads about 28MB of model assets on first run and is usually cached by the browser.

items.question: Which watermark areas work best?
items.answer: Plain backgrounds, gradients, empty screenshot areas, and simple textures work best. Complex photo textures, subject details, or large translucent overlays may need several smaller selections.

items.question: Can I choose the output format?
items.answer: Yes. You can export JPG, PNG, or WebP. JPG does not support alpha transparency, so transparent areas are filled with white.

items.question: Can I process any image?
items.answer: Only process images you own or have permission to modify. The tool provides local AI inpainting and fast browser repair only.

items.question: Does Add watermark upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are rendered locally in your browser via Canvas and exported on the spot. Files are never uploaded to a server.

items.question: What kinds of watermarks are supported?
items.answer: Both text and image watermarks. Text watermarks let you tune font, size, color, bold, italic and stroke; image watermarks accept common formats like PNG, JPG and WebP, with adjustable size.

items.question: How can I position the watermark?
items.answer: Three layouts: single, tile and diagonal. In single mode you can snap to a nine-grid position or drag the watermark anywhere on the preview. Tile/diagonal layouts expose horizontal and vertical spacing controls.

items.question: Which output formats can I choose?
items.answer: PNG, JPG, or WebP. JPG and WebP also offer quality controls. JPG does not support transparency; transparent areas are filled with white.

items.question: Does Image to JPG upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are converted locally in your browser with Canvas or a Worker. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Does JPG keep transparent backgrounds?
items.answer: No. JPG does not support transparency, so transparent areas are filled with a white background.

items.question: Which images can be converted to JPG?
items.answer: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and other common browser-decodable image formats are supported.

items.question: Does converting to JPG reduce image quality?
items.answer: JPG is a lossy format. Lower quality creates smaller files and may lose detail. The quality slider lets you balance size and visual quality.

items.question: Does Image to PNG upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are converted locally in your browser with Canvas or a Worker. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Does PNG keep transparent backgrounds?
items.answer: PNG supports transparency. If the source image and browser decoder include transparent pixels, the exported PNG keeps them.

items.question: Which images can be converted to PNG?
items.answer: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and other common browser-decodable image formats are supported.

items.question: Why can PNG files be larger than JPG files?
items.answer: PNG uses lossless compression and supports transparency. It is useful for icons, screenshots, and sharp edges, but photo-like images are often larger than JPG.

items.question: Does Image to WebP upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are converted locally in your browser with Canvas or a Worker. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: What is WebP good for?
items.answer: WebP often keeps good visual quality with smaller file sizes, making it useful for web images, thumbnails, and compressed image assets.

items.question: Which images can be converted to WebP?
items.answer: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and other common browser-decodable image formats are supported.

items.question: Does converting to WebP reduce image quality?
items.answer: WebP can use lossy compression or preserve high quality. The quality slider controls the tradeoff between output size and visual quality.

items.question: Does Image to AVIF upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are converted locally in your browser with Canvas or a Worker. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: What is AVIF good for?
items.answer: AVIF often keeps strong visual quality at smaller file sizes, making it useful for web images, cover images, thumbnails, and image assets that need extra compression.

items.question: Which images can be converted to AVIF?
items.answer: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and other common browser-decodable image formats are supported.

items.question: Does AVIF conversion have browser limits?
items.answer: AVIF encoding depends on browser support. If your browser cannot export AVIF, the page shows an unsupported output message. Use a recent Chrome, Edge, or Firefox release.

items.question: Does Image to Icon upload my files?
items.answer: No. Image loading, scaling, corner radius rendering, ICO/ICNS packaging, and previews all happen locally in your browser.

items.question: Which input images are supported?
items.answer: PNG, JPG, WebP, SVG, BMP, AVIF, and other common browser-decodable image formats are supported.

items.question: What is the difference between ICO and ICNS?
items.answer: ICO is commonly used for Windows icons and favicons, while ICNS is commonly used for macOS app icons. The page also provides a multi-size PNG ZIP for web and PWA assets.

items.question: Can it remove the background directly?
items.answer: Yes. The remove background button runs locally in the browser, creates a transparent PNG, and then continues making the icon from it.

items.question: Does Image to Base64 upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are read and encoded as Base64 locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Can I paste an image?
items.answer: Yes. You can choose an image, drag an image in, or press Ctrl + V to paste an image from the clipboard.

items.question: Does it output raw Base64 or a Data URL?
items.answer: The page shows the full Data URL by default and also provides a button to copy the raw Base64 string.

items.question: Which images can be converted to Base64?
items.answer: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and other common browser-readable image formats are supported.

items.question: Does Base64 to image upload my content?
items.answer: No. Base64 decoding, preview, and download all happen locally in your browser.

items.question: Which Base64 inputs are supported?
items.answer: Full data:image Data URLs are supported, as well as raw image Base64. Raw Base64 is detected from the image file signature.

items.question: Can I drag in a Base64 file?
items.answer: Yes. You can drag in a .txt or .base64 text file, or press Ctrl + V to paste Base64 content directly.

items.question: How is the output image format chosen?
items.answer: When the input includes a MIME type, it is used first. Raw Base64 is detected from PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF, BMP, SVG, AVIF, and similar signatures.

items.question: Does image crop upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are decoded, cropped, and exported locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Can I drag the crop frame?
items.answer: Yes. You can drag the crop frame to move it, and drag its edges or corners to change its size.

items.question: Does crop also resize the image?
items.answer: No. The crop tool exports the selected crop area at its crop dimensions. Use Image resize when you need a specific width or height.

items.question: Can I choose the output format?
items.answer: Yes. You can export JPG, PNG, or WebP. JPG does not support alpha transparency, so transparent areas are filled with white.

items.question: Does image resize upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are decoded, resized, and exported locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Does resizing keep the image ratio?
items.answer: By default, it keeps the original aspect ratio. Entering a width calculates the height, and entering a height calculates the width.

items.question: Does resize crop the image?
items.answer: No. Image resize scales the full image without cutting edges. Use Image crop when you need to select part of an image.

items.question: Can I choose the output format?
items.answer: Yes. You can export JPG, PNG, or WebP. JPG does not support alpha transparency, so transparent areas are filled with white.

items.question: Does image editing upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images are decoded, drawn on, mosaicked, blurred, and exported locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Which drawing tools are supported?
items.answer: Rectangle, ellipse, polyline, brush, marker, text, mosaic, blur, and eraser are supported. Rectangles and ellipses can be stroked or filled.

items.question: Does the eraser remove the original image?
items.answer: No. The eraser deletes annotation objects on the canvas without changing the original image. Mosaic and blur regions can also be selected and deleted, or handled with undo, redo, and reset image.

items.question: Can I choose the output format?
items.answer: Yes. You can export JPG, PNG, or WebP. JPG does not support alpha transparency, so transparent areas are filled with white.

items.question: Does Convert to PDF upload my files?
items.answer: No. Images, text, Markdown, HTML, docx, xlsx, xls, and pptx are converted locally in the browser in this first release.

items.question: Does Office to PDF preserve the original layout?
items.answer: The current browser version extracts docx paragraphs, Excel table rows, and pptx slide text before generating a PDF. It is useful for quick archiving. Complex layouts and legacy doc or ppt files will need a future server-side converter.

items.question: How much EPUB and MOBI support is included?
items.answer: EPUB is read from the book package and XHTML spine order before generating a PDF. MOBI currently supports text extraction from unencrypted legacy MOBI/PalmDOC files; encrypted MOBI, AZW/KF8, and complex Kindle files need a server-side converter.

items.question: Can I convert files in bulk?
items.answer: Yes. Upload multiple files, then download each converted PDF individually or export everything as a ZIP.

items.question: Which PDF tools are planned next?
items.answer: Planned tools include merge, split, compress, image conversion, edit, annotate, sign, watermark, encrypt, decrypt, and OCR.

items.question: Does PDF to Word upload files?
items.answer: No. PDF text extraction, local OCR, and DOCX generation all run in your browser, so files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Can scanned PDFs become editable Word files?
items.answer: Yes. Each page is checked for a reliable text layer. Scanned pages automatically run through browser-local OCR and become editable text with approximate position and size. If OCR finds no text, the full-page image is retained so the page is not lost.

items.question: Will the DOCX keep the original PDF layout?
items.answer: The converter keeps page boundaries, text sizes, and raster images, preserves basic bold and italic styling when the PDF font data exposes it, and approximates the original spacing. OCR pages are reconstructed approximately; complex tables, text wrapping, vector graphics, and specialized fonts may still differ.

items.question: Does Word Count upload my text?
items.answer: No. Character, word, line, paragraph, and byte counts are calculated locally in your browser.

items.question: How are mixed Chinese and English texts counted?
items.answer: The tool shows characters, non-space characters, words, and CJK character counts separately, so it works well for Chinese, English, and mixed text.

items.question: Does Text Diff upload my content?
items.answer: No. The comparison runs locally in your browser, and the two text inputs are not sent to a server.

items.question: Which diff algorithm does Text Diff use?
items.answer: The tool uses the open-source jsdiff algorithm for line-level comparison, then highlights word-level changes inside modified lines.

items.question: Does Markdown to PDF upload my content?
items.answer: No. Markdown parsing, layout, and PDF generation all run locally in your browser.

items.question: Does the PDF support CJK text and multiple pages?
items.answer: Yes. The tool draws text with browser fonts and creates additional pages when the content exceeds one page.

items.question: Is the exported HTML a complete file?
items.answer: Yes. It includes a doctype, title, responsive viewport, and clean article styles, so it can be opened directly in a browser.

items.question: Will raw HTML inside Markdown execute?
items.answer: No. Raw HTML is escaped, unsafe link protocols are removed, and the preview runs in a restricted environment.

items.question: Does Subtitle Maker upload media or subtitle files?
items.answer: No. Media preview, LRC/SRT/VTT parsing, editing, and export all run locally in your browser. Files are not uploaded to a server.

items.question: Which subtitle formats are supported?
items.answer: SRT, WebVTT, and LRC are supported. You can upload a file or paste subtitle text directly and parse it.

items.question: Can I calibrate timing while media plays?
items.answer: Yes. Upload audio or video, select a subtitle row, and set its start or end time from the current playback position.

items.question: Can I convert between LRC, SRT, and VTT?
items.answer: Yes. After parsing subtitles, switch the output format and export. The tool generates timing codes for the selected target format.

about.title: About ToolGarden
about.meta_description: Learn why ToolGarden builds privacy-first browser-local tools, how the suite works, and how its technical guides are maintained.
about.intro: ToolGarden is a collection of practical web tools designed to process everyday developer and document workflows in the browser whenever the platform can do the work safely and reliably.

sections.title: Why ToolGarden exists
paragraphs: Many online utilities require an upload even when the same transformation can run on the user's device. ToolGarden aims to reduce that unnecessary data movement while keeping useful workflows easy to access.
The site covers JSON, images, PDFs, audio, text, QR codes, subtitles, and related utilities. The tool registry is the source of truth for official tools, navigation, discovery, and search metadata.

sections.title: How browser-local processing works
paragraphs: Supported inputs are decoded and transformed by browser APIs, JavaScript, Web Workers, WebAssembly, or locally executed models. Some advanced tools download code, model, font, or runtime assets before processing can begin, but the selected source file is not sent to a ToolGarden processing API.
Page analytics are a separate data flow from tool processing and are described in the Privacy Policy.

sections.title: How guides are maintained
paragraphs: Technical articles are written for practical use and linked to the relevant tools and topic pillars. Material changes should update the visible modified date. Security, privacy, standards, and compliance claims are reviewed conservatively and should point readers to primary sources where appropriate.
items: Examples should use synthetic data rather than real credentials.
Privacy claims distinguish local tool input from page telemetry.
Compliance articles explain limitations instead of promising automatic certification.

sections.title: Who maintains this site
paragraphs: ToolGarden is maintained by one developer. There is no company entity, no sales team and no support rota, and that should shape what you reasonably expect of it: features and fixes land as maintainer time allows, email usually gets a reply within a few working days, and no service level is promised.

Display advertising covers the domain and bandwidth; the tools themselves are free and need no account. Advertising and tool processing are independent of each other; ad scripts do not touch the files you put into a tool, and the privacy policy sets out exactly how the two data flows are separated.

sections.title: What gets added here
paragraphs: There is one admission test: can this job be done end to end in the browser, with a result that is actually usable? If a feature needs server compute, a private API or a paid third-party service to reach usable quality, it does not ship here; rather than shipping a version that visibly is not good enough.
items: Preference goes to single-task tools with a clear input and output that fit on one screen.
Tools involving model inference; background and watermark removal, upscaling, OCR, transcription, stem splitting; use only open-source models that run in-browser.
When one job has several format paths, each format gets its own tool rather than one universal entry point, because the edge cases differ per format.
Nothing that requires an account, requires an upload to work, or produces results you cannot verify locally.

sections.title: How the content is kept current
paragraphs: Tool descriptions, format tables and stated limits are updated alongside the implementation. When browser capabilities, dependency versions or model behaviour change and make an earlier description inaccurate, the description currently on the page is the authoritative one.

If you find documentation that contradicts actual behaviour, a format claim that is wrong, or a conclusion that has gone stale, say so through the contact page with the page URL. Corrections take priority over new features.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.meta_description: Understand which ToolGarden data stays in your browser, which analytics services receive page telemetry, and how local storage and models are used.
privacy.intro: ToolGarden is built around browser-local tool processing. This policy explains the important distinction between the text or files you process and the page-level telemetry generated while visiting the site.

sections.title: Tool inputs and local processing
paragraphs: Text, files, images, PDFs, audio, and other inputs selected inside supported tools are intended to be processed on your device and are not uploaded to a ToolGarden processing server. Tool workspaces are explicitly marked for Microsoft Clarity masking, and standard input fields are masked by Clarity in all masking modes.

Some tools download JavaScript, WebAssembly, fonts, codecs, or machine-learning model assets. Network access for those assets is not an upload of your selected source file. You can inspect the browser Network panel when a workflow requires independent verification.

sections.title: Analytics and page telemetry
paragraphs: ToolGarden uses Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity across the site, and Baidu Analytics on Chinese-language routes. These services may receive page URLs and titles, approximate location, browser and device information, identifiers, performance diagnostics, and interaction events such as clicks, scrolling, and page navigation.

Analytics data is handled under each provider's terms, controls, and retention settings. Do not place personal data or secrets in page URLs. ToolGarden does not intentionally send filenames, tool input values, or generated output values as custom analytics events.

sections.title: Advertising and consent
paragraphs: ToolGarden uses Google AdSense to fund the public service. Google and its advertising partners may use cookies or similar storage to deliver and measure ads, limit repeated ads, detect invalid traffic, and, where permitted by your choices and applicable law, personalize advertising.

Ad requests can include the page URL, IP address, browser and device information, advertising or consent identifiers, and interaction data related to an ad. ToolGarden does not intentionally send the text, files, images, audio, or generated output you process inside a tool as advertising data. Where a consent message is shown, you can accept, reject, or adjust the available advertising choices.

sections.title: Browser storage and caching
paragraphs: The site may use browser cache, service-worker storage, cookies, or local storage for offline assets, preferences, tool-specific persistence such as whiteboard state, and strictly necessary security functions such as abuse prevention and traffic routing at the CDN edge. These items remain under your browser profile and can be removed through your browser's site-data controls, although removing required security data may cause it to be set again on a later request.

sections.title: Your choices and questions
paragraphs: Browser privacy controls, content blockers, and site-data settings may limit analytics and stored data, although blocking required scripts or assets can affect tool functionality. Contact ToolGarden if you have a privacy question or believe sensitive data has been exposed.

sections.title: Availability and warranties

sections.title: Your files and your rights
paragraphs: The files you put into a tool remain yours. The site acquires no rights over them, claims none, and for the supported tools could not acquire them, because the content never leaves your device; the privacy policy identifies which tools those are.

In return, it is on you to confirm you are entitled to process the material. Font subsetting is bound by font licensing, watermark removal does not change who owns an image's copyright, and PDF decryption applies only to documents you already have the right to open. Technically possible is not the same as permitted, and that judgement is yours.

Advertising revenue does not change how any tool processes data or where that data goes.

The site is built on a substantial amount of open-source software; including FFmpeg, pdf-lib, pdfjs, Excalidraw, tldraw, Mind Elixir and Transformers.js, plus the model files they depend on. Each remains under its own licence, unchanged by being used here.

The technical explanations, format comparisons and stated limits on these pages are engineering descriptions. They are not legal, security, medical, financial or compliance advice. security.title: Security
security.meta_description: Learn about ToolGarden security boundaries, browser-local processing, dependency controls, and how to report a potential vulnerability.
security.intro: ToolGarden reduces server-side exposure by processing supported tool inputs in the browser, while recognizing that delivered code, dependencies, analytics, and the user's own device remain part of the security model.

sections.title: Security boundaries
paragraphs: No-upload processing removes a remote file-processing step, but it does not make a compromised browser, extension, device, dependency, or website harmless. Use a maintained browser, review unusually sensitive workflows, and work on copies of important files.

sections.title: Engineering controls
paragraphs: The project uses a centralized tool registry, pure utility functions, static export hardening, a Content Security Policy, dependency review, and automated lint, type, build, and regression checks. Large libraries and models are loaded only by the tools that need them where practical.
items: Tool workspace content is marked for Clarity masking.
Source maps are removed from production exports.
Hashed application assets are cached separately from navigational documents.
Security-sensitive dependencies are upgraded or isolated when a compatible fix is available.

sections.title: Report a vulnerability
paragraphs: Send a concise report with the affected URL, impact, reproduction steps, browser version, and any safe proof of concept. Do not include live credentials, private user files, or destructive test data. Please allow reasonable time for investigation before public disclosure.

sections.title: What browser-local processing actually guarantees
paragraphs: "No upload" means precisely this: content you supply through the file picker, by drag and drop, or by pasting is never sent to any ToolGarden endpoint. It does not mean the page makes no network requests; the page itself, its JavaScript, its fonts, and the model files some tools need all come down from the network.

Put differently, this boundary is verifiable. Open the network panel in your browser's developer tools and exercise any tool: you should see downloads of static assets and model files, and no request carrying your file's contents. That is more reliable than any written promise, and you are welcome to check it yourself.

sections.title: Where data can persist on your device
paragraphs: Most tools process purely in memory and release everything when the tab closes. A few exceptions leave traces locally, and you should know about them:
items: Canvas tools; Whiteboard, Excalidraw Board, Mind Map; store their content in browser local storage so a refresh does not lose your work.
Model files are cached after first download to avoid fetching them again; these are public model weights and contain none of your data.
A Service Worker caches the pages and static assets that make offline use possible.
All of the above can be removed at once with your browser's "clear site data" control.

sections.title: Where this model does not help
paragraphs: Local processing removes one class of risk; your file sitting on someone else's server. It does nothing about a device that is already compromised, a browser extension reading page content, residue on a shared or public machine, or somebody simply reading your screen.

If your threat model includes any of those, or your organisation requires specific data to be handled inside an audited environment, use offline software that meets that requirement rather than any web tool; this one included.

contact.title: Contact ToolGarden
contact.meta_description: Contact ToolGarden about tool feedback, privacy questions, content corrections, accessibility, or responsible security reports.
contact.intro: Feedback is welcome for broken workflows, browser compatibility, privacy questions, article corrections, accessibility, and responsible security reports.

sections.title: What to include
paragraphs: Include the page URL, browser and operating-system version, expected result, actual result, and steps that reproduce the issue. Use synthetic sample data whenever possible.

sections.title: Protect sensitive information
paragraphs: Do not email passwords, API keys, session cookies, identity documents, confidential files, or unredacted customer data. For a security report, provide the minimum safe proof needed to understand the issue.

sections.title: Response times and what to expect
paragraphs: The site is maintained by one developer; there is no support team. Email usually gets a reply within a few working days. Security reports are handled first; feature suggestions are recorded without a promised delivery date. To be unambiguous: no service level is offered, and there is no phone or instant-messaging support.

sections.title: Sorting by type
paragraphs: Putting the type in your subject line measurably speeds things up:
items: A tool errors or returns the wrong result; include the page URL, browser and OS version, steps to reproduce, and a sample file you are able to share.
A correction; documentation that contradicts behaviour, an incorrect format claim, a conclusion that has aged out. Name the page and the passage.
A privacy question; uncertainty about where a particular tool's data goes, or behaviour that looks inconsistent with the privacy policy.
Accessibility; keyboard navigation, screen readers, contrast or text size. Tell us which assistive technology you use.
A security report; read the reporting requirements on the security page first, and include only the minimum evidence needed to understand the issue.

sections.title: Check here first; most questions need no email
paragraphs: The following already have answers on the site, and looking is usually faster than waiting for a reply:
items: "Will my file be uploaded?"; every tool page's Supported range and limits table has a Where it runs row stating that tool's data flow. The privacy policy and security page cover it in general.

"Why is it slow, or failing?"; the model-based tools (background and watermark removal, upscaling, OCR, transcription, stem splitting) download tens of megabytes on first use and run inference on your device. Each tool page's What to know before you start lists its real limits.

"The output does not match the original"; the comparison table on each tool page states whether an operation is lossless or lossy and what it discards. PDF to Word, image compression and audio transcoding are especially worth reading first.
"Which formats are supported?"; the limits table on each tool page enumerates accepted inputs and outputs, which beats guessing from search results.

sections.title: About feature suggestions
paragraphs: Suggestions are welcome, but please say whether the job can be done end to end in the browser. That is the site's only admission test: anything needing server compute, a private API or a paid third-party service to reach usable quality will not ship, because it contradicts the premise that your files stay on your device.
Suggestions already under consideration get recorded, but with no promised date; there is one maintainer, and scheduling follows available time.

sections.title: What email cannot help with
paragraphs: A few kinds of request cannot be answered, stated here so you are not left waiting:
items: Processing files on your behalf. Please do not attach files; the tools are for you to run, and doing it for you defeats the point of local processing.
Recovering passwords. A PDF whose open password is lost cannot be opened, which is what encryption is for.
Business partnerships, advertising placement, link exchanges and sponsored content; none of these receive a reply.
Requests for source code, deployment details or keys framed as a "compliance check" or "security assessment" are not answered.

lead: Every tool on ToolGarden starts from one premise: if the browser can do the work itself, the file does not go to a server. JSON parsing, image codecs, PDF page reassembly, audio transcoding, OCR and background-removal models all run in-page now, via Canvas, Web Workers, WebAssembly and local models.

The practical consequence is that you can drop an API response containing tokens, an unsigned contract, a scanned ID or an unpublished manuscript straight into a tool, because none of it leaves this device.

choosing.title: Find it by data type
choosing.detail: The top navigation groups tools by JSON, image, audio, PDF, text, file merging, encoding, QR codes and subtitles. When you know what kind of file you are holding, the category page is the fastest way in.

choosing.title: Find it by action
choosing.detail: Within a category, tools are named after the action; convert, compress, merge, split, diff, validate, extract. Search matches action words directly, so typing "merge" lists the merge tool for every format.

choosing.detail: Every category page carries a "choosing between these tools" section and a format comparison table, and every tool page has steps, a worked input/output example and its limits. Reading the category page first saves redoing the job after picking the wrong format.

choosing.title: Curious how it works
choosing.detail: The blog covers in-browser media processing, model inference and format specifications, and tool pages link down to the relevant deep-dive guide.

comparison.caption: Local processing differs from upload-based tools in more than privacy; the capability limits differ too, which is what tells you when to reach for desktop software instead.
rows: The file stays on your device; only code and models come down the wire
The file must be uploaded, after which retention and deletion are the operator's policy
Bounded by browser memory; very large files can fail
Bounded by server limits, and usually handles more
Depends on your device; transcoding is fast, model inference is slow
Depends on server capacity, and is usually more predictable
Most tools work offline once their assets are cached

notes: Every tool is free and needs no account. The site does count page visits to learn which tools get used; that is a separate data flow from what you put into a tool, and the privacy policy spells out the distinction.

The trade-off for local processing is that the compute and the memory are yours. Files up to tens of megabytes are generally fine, but very long media, PDFs with a great many pages, and AI tools that download tens of megabytes of model can be slow or fail outright on modest hardware or a weak connection. Desktop or command-line software is the better choice there.
Most conversions are lossy or not fully reversible. Always keep the original file, and check the output before a converted result goes into a real process.

hub_article.notes: Limits that apply across this category

lead: These tools all serve one goal: turning JSON from machine-readable into something you can read, edit and verify. Debugging an API mostly means formatting and minifying; config files often need comments and trailing commas repaired; integration work means converting between JSON, YAML, XML, CSV and Excel; and diagnosing a production issue usually comes down to diffing two responses or pulling one field out with JSONPath.
All parsing happens in your browser, so you can paste a real response containing tokens, phone numbers or order IDs without redacting it first for some online service.

choosing.title: You just need to see the structure
choosing.detail: Use JSON Formatter. It accepts strict JSON, commented JSONC and JSON5 alike, and renders a collapsible tree; the fastest way to find a field inside a single-line response.

choosing.title: The text will not parse at all
choosing.detail: Start with JSON Repair. Comments, trailing commas, single quotes, unquoted keys and escape backslashes picked up from log lines are all its job. Fix it there, then hand the result to the other tools.

choosing.title: You need a different data format
choosing.detail: JSON ↔ YAML suits config files, JSON ↔ XML suits legacy APIs, JSON → CSV / Excel hands an array to non-technical colleagues, and JSON → TypeScript freezes a response into a type.

choosing.title: You need to validate, not just view
choosing.detail: JSON Schema Generator infers constraints from a sample, JSON Schema Validator checks data against those constraints and reports error paths, JSONPath Query extracts deep fields by expression, and JSON Stats reports depth, key count and type distribution.

notes: JSON numbers parse as JavaScript numbers, which represent integers exactly only up to 2^53-1. Snowflake IDs, order numbers and account balances should travel as strings at the transport layer, otherwise any JavaScript-based parser loses the last digits. That is a property of the format and the language, not a defect in one tool.

Conversion is lossy. Comments, metadata beyond key order, XML attributes and namespaces, and CSV types do not necessarily survive a round trip. Keep the original file before you use a converted result in a real process.

lead: Most image work does not actually need a server. Canvas and WebCodecs decode and re-encode the common formats, WebAssembly runs the compression algorithms, and WASM or WebGPU can run the models behind background removal, watermark removal, upscaling and OCR. That premise is what this whole category is built on.

So the photos, ID scans and screenshots you open never leave your device. Background and watermark removal do download open-source model files into the browser first; the model comes from the network, the image you picked does not.

choosing.title: You need a smaller file
choosing.detail: Image Compress re-encodes at a chosen quality and keeps the original format by default. If the goal is page load speed, switching the output to WebP or AVIF usually saves over thirty percent against a JPG of the same visual quality.

choosing.title: You need different dimensions, not different quality
choosing.detail: Image Resize scales proportionally, Image Crop takes a region by dragging a box, and Image Upscale is for cases where the result still has to look sharp. Scaling down loses little; scaling up has a model invent detail rather than recover real detail.

choosing.title: You need to change the content itself
choosing.detail: Remove Background exports a transparent PNG, ID Photo Maker crops to standard sizes and swaps the backdrop after removing the background, Remove Watermark inpaints the region you mark, and Image Editor handles redaction, blur and annotation.

choosing.title: You need information out of an image
choosing.detail: OCR extracts text, Color Picker reads HEX / RGB / HSL from any pixel, and EXIF Viewer shows capture settings and location data; and can strip all of it before you export.

comparison.caption: The output-format trade-off. Picking wrong can multiply the file size, or silently drop the transparency you needed.
rows: Photographs and broad gradients; the most compatible option
Screenshots, line art, anything needing a transparent background
General web use; clearly smaller than JPG or PNG at equal quality
Smallest files, but slow to encode and unsupported by older browsers

notes: Re-encoding stacks losses. Compressing a JPG repeatedly, or converting out and back, discards a little more detail every round; always start from the original, never from the previous output.

Stripping EXIF removes location, device model and capture time together. That is what you want before publishing, but it also means the information is gone for good. Save a copy of the original first if you need it on file.

Background removal, watermark removal, upscaling and OCR depend on model files. The first run downloads tens of megabytes, which is noticeably slow; and sometimes fails; on low-end devices or weak connections.

lead: These tools run FFmpeg compiled to WebAssembly, so format conversion, trimming, merging, speed changes and resampling all happen in the browser instead of on a server. Audio-to-text runs an open-source Whisper model in-page, and stem splitting runs its separation model the same way.
The cost is that the compute is yours: transcribing or splitting a few minutes of audio can take a long wait, where the same file converts format in seconds.

choosing.title: You only need a different format
choosing.detail: Audio to MP3 is the most compatible and the smallest; Audio to WAV gives you uncompressed PCM, which is what you want before further processing or import into a DAW. To pull sound out of a video, use Audio Extract.

choosing.title: You need to cut or join
choosing.detail: Audio Trim takes a section by start and end time, Audio Merge joins several files of different formats into one MP3, and Remove Silence cuts the blank stretches automatically; useful on raw recordings.

choosing.title: You need to change how it sounds or how big it is
choosing.detail: Change Volume and Change Speed alter playback directly. Audio Compress and Change Bitrate reduce size by lowering the bitrate. Change Sample Rate is for matching what a target device or application requires.

choosing.title: You need the sound turned into something else
choosing.detail: Audio to Text produces a transcript, Split Stems separates a song into vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and other, Text to Speech reads text aloud with the browser's own synthesiser, and Voice Recorder captures straight from the microphone.

comparison.caption: Bitrate sets the balance between size and quality. Rough guidance for common MP3 settings; the real difference depends on your material and listening setup.
rows: Intelligible, but detail is clearly gone
Speech only, meeting recordings, podcast drafts
Music where you want maximum fidelity

notes: MP3 is lossy, and re-encoding cannot bring back high frequencies that are already gone. Converting a 128 kbps file to 320 kbps only makes it bigger; for fidelity you have to start from a lossless source.
FFmpeg in the browser reads the whole file into memory, so large inputs; especially extracting audio from a long video; can fail for lack of memory. Cut the source shorter when that happens.
Audio-to-text and stem splitting download a model and then do heavy computation. Time scales with audio length and device speed, and phones may not finish longer material at all.

lead: PDF was designed to look identical on every device, and the price of that is a file which records where each glyph sits on the page rather than what the document means. That explains exactly where this category's abilities end: page-level work; merging, splitting, extracting, reordering, watermarking, encrypting; is reliable and lossless, while converting to Word means reconstructing structure that was never stored.
Everything runs in the browser, so contracts, invoices and scanned documents never go to a third-party service.

choosing.title: Page-level organisation
choosing.detail: Merge PDF joins documents with drag-to-reorder, Split PDF cuts by page range, Extract Pages pulls out the pages you want, and Organize PDF reorders, duplicates and deletes pages before export. None of these re-render content, so all are lossless.

choosing.title: Converting to another format
choosing.detail: Convert to PDF accepts Word, Excel, PowerPoint, EPUB, images, Markdown and HTML. PDF to Word produces an editable DOCX. PDF to Image exports each page as PNG or JPG; handy for slides, or for people without a reader.

choosing.title: Controlling who can open it and do what
choosing.detail: PDF Encrypt sets an open password and can restrict printing and copying, or remove a password you know. PDF Watermark overlays text with nine-point positioning, tiling, diagonal placement and adjustable opacity.

comparison.caption: How faithfully each operation preserves the original; worth checking before you pick one.
rows: Only the organisation of page objects changes
Bookmarks and some form fields may not follow the pages
A layer is drawn over the original page
The watermark is an editable layer, so it is not tamper-proofing
Only permissions and encryption settings change
Permission flags rely on the reader honouring them
Paragraphs and styles are inferred from glyph positions
Complex layouts, tables and columns need a human pass

notes: A scan is fundamentally an image. If the PDF came from a camera or scanner it has no text layer, so converting to Word or copying text returns nothing; run OCR first in that case.

PDF permission flags such as no-printing and no-copying are declarations addressed to the reader application, and they hold only as long as the reader honours them. Use an open password when the content genuinely needs protecting.
Local processing is bounded by browser memory. Files with very many pages, or lots of high-resolution images, can fail; split them first and process the parts.

lead: Joining several files of the same kind sounds trivial, but "joining" means something different in every format: PDF concatenates page objects, Word has to merge document streams and stylesheets, Excel must decide between one combined sheet and one sheet per source, CSV has to handle repeated headers, and images need a choice between one tall strip and one page each.
Each tool here implements the logic its format actually needs, all in the browser, so the files you are merging are never uploaded.

choosing.title: Documents
choosing.detail: Merge PDF preserves the original layout most reliably. Word Merge outputs a single DOCX, resolving style conflicts in favour of the earlier document. PPT Merge joins slides from several decks. RTF Merge suits rich text exported from older editors.

choosing.title: Spreadsheets
choosing.detail: Excel Merge lets you either pool all data into one sheet or give each source file its own sheet. CSV Merge appends rows, so check that the column order matches across your sources.

choosing.title: Plain text and images
choosing.detail: TXT Merge and Markdown Merge concatenate in list order, which is how you reassemble a draft split by chapter. Image Merge stacks images into one tall PNG, or composes them into a PDF with one image per page.

comparison.caption: How ordering and structure are handled, format by format.
rows: Bookmarks and form fields may not survive
Same-named styles resolve to the earlier document
Rows appended, or one sheet per source
Mismatched column order silently misaligns data
Stacked vertically, or one per page
Differing widths leave blank margins in the strip

notes: Check that your sources share the same structure before merging. CSV and Excel are the dangerous ones: one extra column, one missing column, or a different column order misaligns the result; and nothing reports an error, so you have to verify it yourself.
Merging is one-way; there is no unmerge. Keep the originals. PDFs can be cut apart again by page range with Split PDF, but for the other formats the boundary information no longer exists once merged.

lead: This category works on plain text itself: counting how much of it there is, finding what changed between two drafts, turning Markdown into something deliverable, and lifting text back out of an image.
Nothing is uploaded; comparison and counting both run in the browser; so unpublished manuscripts, draft contracts and records containing personal data are all fair game.

choosing.title: You need to know the length
choosing.detail: Word Count reports characters, words, lines, paragraphs, sentences and byte size at once. The gap between counting Chinese by character and English by word is visible here, and a submission limit almost always means one specific one of these numbers.

choosing.title: You need to see what changed
choosing.detail: Text Diff highlights insertions, deletions and edits at both line and word level; for contract versions, translation review and manuscript revisions. If both sides are JSON, JSON Diff gives you differences by field instead of by line.

choosing.title: You need to ship the Markdown
choosing.detail: Markdown to PDF generates a downloadable PDF locally with mixed-script text and automatic pagination. Markdown to HTML emits complete HTML you can preview, copy and download into a CMS or an email.

choosing.title: The text is inside an image
choosing.detail: Run Image OCR first to extract it, then bring the result to the tools above for counting or comparison.

notes: There is no single correct way to count words. CJK text is normally counted by character and English by whitespace-delimited word, and whether punctuation, spaces and numerals count varies by publisher. Follow whatever definition your target platform gives; the several figures here exist so you can match any of them.

Text Diff is a literal comparison by line and by word; it does not understand meaning. Paraphrases and reordered clauses show up as large differences, while a critical change to a number or a unit may show as a single character. Important documents still need a human read.

Markdown to PDF renders with the fonts available in your browser, so output depends on your system fonts. When the typography has to match across devices, treat the generated PDF as the authority rather than the on-screen preview.

comparison.caption: How a word count is defined causes more confusion in this category than anything else. The same text can differ by more than a factor of two between rules.
rows: Each character and punctuation mark counts as 1
Each letter, space and mark counts as 1
Almost the same as with spaces
Clearly lower than the with-spaces figure
Some submission systems and ad-copy limits
Usually equals the character count, since CJK has no word spaces
Split on whitespace, roughly a sixth of the character count
English academic writing and per-word rates
A CJK character normally takes 3 bytes
Database column lengths and payload limits

lead: What lands here does not fit the categories above but runs locally just the same: three canvas tools; a whiteboard, a hand-drawn-style board and a mind map; plus a font subsetting tool.
Canvas content is stored in your browser, and font subsetting reads the font file into memory and cuts a subset out of it. Neither uploads anything.

choosing.title: You want a board you can draw and stick notes on
choosing.detail: Whiteboard is built on tldraw, with shapes, freehand drawing, sticky notes, images, multiple pages and export; good for working through a process or capturing a meeting as it happens.

choosing.title: You want the look of a sketch
choosing.detail: Excalidraw Board produces hand-drawn strokes, which suits architecture sketches and explanatory diagrams: the deliberate roughness tells the reader this is a draft that will still change.

choosing.title: You want to organise a hierarchy
choosing.detail: Mind Map is built on Mind Elixir, edits the node tree directly, and exports to a Markdown outline you can carry on writing in a document.

choosing.title: You want a smaller web font
choosing.detail: Font Subset pulls only the characters you specify out of a TTF or WOFF, producing a far smaller font. CJK fonts run to several megabytes; embedding only the few dozen glyphs actually used typically brings that down to tens of kilobytes.

notes: Canvas content lives in browser local storage, so clearing browsing data, switching browsers or moving to another device makes it disappear. Export anything you care about to a file.

Font subsetting is bounded by licensing. Not every font may be redistributed or embedded in a web page, so check the licence terms before processing a commercial font; technically possible is not the same as permitted.

comparison.caption: All three canvas tools exist to get an idea drawn, but they suit different stages; and the wrong one misleads the reader about your intent.

Diagrams and meeting records that should look finished
Free canvas with grouping and layer order
Draft stage, where deliberate roughness invites changes
A tree; every node has one parent
Clear hierarchical breakdowns, exportable to Markdown
Not a canvas tool; it processes font files
